#57800. Vision Language Models (Better, faster, stronger)

📅 12 May 2025 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4348 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Vision Language Models (Better, faster, stronger)

📅 12 May 2025 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4348 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, vision Language Models (VLMs) are the talk of the town.
  • Models have become smaller yet more powerful.
  • In this blog post, we’ll take a look back and unpack everything that happened with vision language models the past year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vision Language Models (VLMs) are the talk of the town. In a previous blog post (from April 2024), we talked a lot about VLMs. A major chunk was about LLaVA, the first successful and easily reproducible open-source vision language model, along with tips on how to discover, evaluate, and fine-tune open models.

Since then, so much has changed. Models have become smaller yet more powerful. We've seen the rise of upcoming architectures and capabilities (reasoning, agency, long video understanding, etc.). In parallel, entirely new paradigms, such as multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and multimodal agents have taken shape.

In this blog post, we’ll take a look back and unpack everything that happened with vision language models the past year. You’ll discover key changes, emerging trends, and notable developments.

We highly recommend reading the first blog post if you want a good primer on how vision language models work.

It has been revealed that in this section, we will look at the new types of VLMs. While some are absolutely new, others are improved versions of previous research.

Any-to-any models, as the name suggests, are models that can take in any modality and output any modality (image, text, audio). They do it by aligning the modalities, where an input from one modality can be translated to another (e.g. the word “dog” would be associated with an image of a dog, or with the utterance of the word).

In a recent development, these models have multiple encoders (one for each modality) and then fuse the embeddings together to create a shared representation space. The decoders (multiple or single) use the shared latent space as input and decode into the modality of choice. Earliest attempt to build any-to-any models is Chameleon by Meta, which can take in image and text and output image and text. Meta didn’t release the image generation capability in this model, so Alpha-VLLM released Lumina-mGPT, which has built image generation on top of Chameleon.

The latest and most capable any-to-any model, Qwen 2.5 Omni (figure below) is a good example to understand the architecture of an any-to-any model.

Qwen2.5-Omni employs a novel "Thinker-Talker" architecture, where the "Thinker" handles text generation, and the "Talker" produces natural speech responses in a streaming manner. MiniCPM-o 2.6, an 8B parameter multimodal model is capable of understanding and generating content across vision, speech, and language modalities. Janus-Pro-7B, introduced by DeepSeek AI, is a unified multimodal model that excels in both understanding and generating content across modalities. It features a decoupled visual encoding architecture, separating the processes for understanding and generation.

We suspect an uptick in the number of such models in the coming years. It is a well-known intuition that multimodal learning is the only way we can learn deep representations better. We have curated some any-to-any models and demos in this collection.

Industry observers note that reasoning models are models that can solve complex problems. We saw them first with large language models, and now vision language models. Until 2025, there was only one open-source multimodal reasoning model, QVQ-72B-preview by Qwen. It was an experimental model that was developed by the Alibaba Qwen team and came with many disclaimers.

This year there’s another player, Kimi-VL-A3B-Thinking by the Moonshot AI team. It consists of MoonViT (SigLIP-so-400M) as the image encoder and a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) decoder with 16B total parameters and only 2.8B active parameters. The model is a long chain-of-thought fine-tuned and further aligned (reinforcement learning) version of the Kimi-VL base vision language model. You can try the model here.

The authors also released an instruction fine-tuned version called Kimi-VL-A3B-Instruct.

According to recent reports, the model can take in long videos, PDFs, screenshots and more. It has agentic capabilities as well.

The community used to scale intelligence through the number of parameters, and then high-quality synthetic data. After a certain point, the benchmarks saturated and scaling models had diminishing returns. The community went to shrink larger models through various methods, like distillation. This makes sense because it reduces compute costs, simplifies deployment, and unlocks use cases like local execution, enhancing data privacy.

Recent findings suggest that when we say small vision language models we often refer to models with less than 2B parameters that can be run on consumer GPUs. SmolVLM is a good example model family for smaller vision language models. Instead of shrinking larger models, the authors went all the way and tried to fit models into tiny number of parameters like 256M, 500M and 2.2B. SmolVLM2, for instance, attempted to solve video understanding in these sizes and found 500M to be a good trade-off. At Hugging Face, we have built an iPhone application, HuggingSnap, to demonstrate that these model sizes can achieve video understanding on consumer devices.

Another striking model is gemma3-4b-it by Google DeepMind. It’s particularly exciting as it’s one of the smallest multimodal models to have 128k token context window, and supports 140+ languages. The model comes with the Gemma 3 family of models, with its largest model ranking first on Chatbot Arena at the time. The largest model was then distilled to a 1B variant.

Lastly, although not the smallest, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct is worth noting. The model can do various tasks ranging from localization (object detection and pointing), to document understanding, to agentic tasks; with context length up to 32k tokens.

According to recent reports, you can use small models through MLX and Llama.cpp integrations. For MLX, assuming you have it installed, you can get started with SmolVLM-500M-Instruct with this one liner:.

You can get started with using gemma-3-4b-it model in GGUF format with llama.cpp through CLI with this one-liner:.

You can also serve the same model as follows.

We would like to give a shoutout to moondream2 and Florence-2 as they're the earliest attempts for smallest vision language models. In this blog, we are covering primarily newer models (mostly models that came out after April 2024).

In a recent development, mixture of Expert (MoEs) models offer an alternative to dense architectures by dynamically selecting and activating only the most relevant sub-models, termed "experts", to process a given input data segment. This selective activation (done by a router) mechanism has demonstrated the potential to substantially enhance model performance and operational efficiency while utilizing fewer computational resources.

Sources indicate that moEs are faster at inference than their similar parameter-dense counterparts because of the selective activation of a smaller slice of the network. They also converge quickly during training. Every good thing comes with a cost, as MoEs need more memory cost due to the entire model being on the GPU, even if a smaller chunk is used.

According to recent reports, in the widely adopted Transformer architecture, MoE layers are most commonly integrated by replacing the standard Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers within each Transformer block. Dense networks use the entire model to run an inference, while similarly sized MoE networks selectively activate some experts. This helps in better compute utilization and faster inference.

In a recent development, vision language models that have mixture-of-experts decoders seem to have enhanced performance. For instance, Kimi-VL as of now is the most advanced open reasoning model that has a mixture-of-experts decoder. Mixture-of-Experts show promising results with MoE-LLaVA's focus on efficiency and hallucination reduction and DeepSeek-VL2's broad multimodal capabilities too. The latest version of Llama (Llama 4) is an MoE with vision capabilities. MoE as a decoder is a promising research area, and we suspect an increase in models like these.

To get a nice understanding of MoEs we recommend reading this fantastic article.

In a recent development, VLMs are even making their mark in the field of robotics! There, they are known as Vision-language-action models (VLA). But don't be fooled, those are mainly VLMs with a little moustache and hat. VLAs take images and text instructions, and return text indicating actions for the robot to take directly. VLAs extend vision language models by adding action and state tokens to interact with and control physical environments. These extra tokens represent the system’s internal state (how it perceives the environment), actions (what it does based on commands), and time-related information (like the order of steps in a task). These tokens are appended to the vision language input to generate actions or policy.

VLAs are usually fine-tuned on top of a base VLM. Some people extend this definition further and define VLAs as any model interacting visually with a real or digital world. In this definition, VLAs can do UI navigation or be used in agentic workflows. But many people believe those applications fall in the VLM domain.

Great examples of VLAs are π0 and π0-FAST, the first robotics foundation models by Physical Intelligence, ported to Hugging Face’s LeRobot library. These models are trained across 7 robotics platforms and 68 unique tasks. They show strong zero-shot and fine-tuned performance on complex, real-world activities such as laundry folding, table bussing, grocery bagging, box assembly, and object retrieval.

According to recent reports, GR00T N1 is NVIDIA’s open VLA foundation model for generalist humanoid robots. It understands images and language, and turns them into actions, like moving its arms or following instructions, thanks to a system that combines smart reasoning with real-time movement control. GR00T N1 also builds on the LeRobot dataset format, the open standard created to simplify sharing and training on robot demonstrations.

Now that we’ve looked at the latest VLM model innovations, let’s explore how more established capabilities have evolved.

As we’ve seen in earlier sections, VLMs enable generalization over traditional computer vision tasks. Models can now take in images and a variety of prompts, such as open-ended text, and output structured text with localization tokens (for detection, segmentation and more).

Last year, PaliGemma was the first model to attempt solving these tasks. The model takes in an image and text, where text is a description of an object of interest, along with a task prefix. The text prompt looks like “segment striped cat” or “detect bird on the roof”.

Recent findings suggest that for detection, the model outputs the bounding box coordinates as tokens. For segmentation, on the other hand, the model outputs detection tokens and segmentation tokens. These segmentation tokens aren’t all the segmented pixel coordinates, but codebook indices that are decoded by a variational autoencoder trained to decode these tokens into valid segmentation masks (as shown in the figure below).

In a recent development, many models have been introduced to do localization tasks after PaliGemma. Late last year, an upgraded version of PaliGemma, PaliGemma 2, appeared with the same capabilities and better performance. Another model that came later was Molmo by Allen AI, which can point to instances with dots and count object instances.

Qwen2.5-VL can also detect, point to, and count objects, and this includes UI elements as objects too!

Vision language models in production require filtering inputs and outputs to prevent jailbreaks and harmful outputs for compliance. Harmful content varies from inputs with violence to sexually explicit content. That’s where multimodal safety models come in: they are used before and after vision language models to filter their inputs and outputs. They are just like LLM safety models but with additional image input.

In early 2025, Google introduced the first open multimodal safety model, ShieldGemma 2. It is built on ShieldGemma, the text-only safety model. This model takes in images and content policies and returns whether an image is safe for a given policy. Policy refers to a criterion in which the image is inappropriate. ShieldGemma 2 can also be used to filter outputs of image generation models.

Recent findings suggest that llama Guard 4 by Meta, is a dense multimodal and multilingual safety model. It is densely pruned from Llama 4 Scout (a multimodal mixture-of-experts) with safety fine tuning.

Recent findings suggest that the model can be used for text-only and multimodal inference. The model can also take in vision language model outputs, complete conversations, and filter them before sending them to the user.

Now let’s look at how Retrieval Augmented Generation has evolved in the multimodal space. RAG for complex documents, usually formatted in PDF, is processed in three steps:.

Industry observers note that A traditional PDF parser consists of multiple elements to preserve the structure and visual elements in the document, such as layout, tables, images, charts, all rendered into a markdown. But this setup can be hard to maintain.

With the rise of vision language models, this issue was addressed: there are now multimodal retrievers and rerankers.

Multimodal retrievers take a stack of PDFs and a query as input and return the most relevant page numbers along with their confidence scores. The scores represent how likely the page contains the answer to the query, or how relevant the query is to the page. This bypasses the brittle parsing step.

The most relevant pages are then fed to the vision language model along with the query, and the VLM generates the answer.

There are two main multimodal retriever architectures:.

In a recent development, DSE models consist of a text encoder and an image encoder, returning a single vector per query. The returned scores are softmax over the dot products of embeddings. They return a single vector per passage.

ColBERT-like models, like ColPali, are also dual encoder models, with a twist: ColPali has a vision language model as an image encoder, and a large language model as a text encoder. These models are inherently not encoders, but the models output embeddings, which are then passed to a “MaxSim”. The outputs are multiple vectors, one for each token, unlike DSE. In MaxSim, the similarity between each text token embedding and each image patch embedding is calculated, and this approach captures nuances better. Due to this reason, ColBERT-like models are less cost-efficient, have better performance.

It has been revealed that below you can see the indexing latency for ColPali. Since it’s just a single model, it’s also easier to maintain.

On Hugging Face Hub, you can find these models under the task “Visual Document Retrieval”.

Recent findings suggest that the most popular benchmark for this task is ViDoRe, which consists of documents in English and French, with documents varying from financial reports, scientific figures to administrative documents. Each example of ViDoRe has the document as image, a query and potential answers. The documents matched with the queries help with contrastive pre-training, so the ViDoRe train set is used to train fresh models.

Vision language models unlock many agentic workflows from chatting with documents to computer use. Here we will cover the latter since it requires more advanced agentic capabilities. Recently, there have been many vision language models releases that understand and operate over UIs. The latest one is UI-TARS-1.5 by ByteDance, which demonstrated great results in operating over browser, computer and phone use. It can also do gameplay with reasoning, and operate in open world games. Another impactful release of this year is MAGMA-8B, it’s a foundation model for both UI navigation and physical interaction with the real world. Moreover, Qwen2.5-VL (especially its 32B variant as it is further trained on agentic tasks) and Kimi-VL reasoning model are good in GUI agentic tasks.

In a recent development, at the beginning of 2025, we introduced smolagents, a new lightweight agentic library that implements the ReAct framework. Shortly after, we implemented vision language support for the library. This integration took place on two use cases:.

The library provides building blocks for the consumers to build their own agentic workflows with image understanding. We provide different scripts and single-line CLI commands to get the users started easily.

Sources indicate that for the first case, assume we want an agent to describe documents (which is not very agentic, but good for minimal use cases). You can initialize the CodeAgent (an agent that writes its own code!) like the following:.

According to recent reports, for the latter use case where we need an agent to get screenshots, we can define a callback to be executed at the end of each ActionStep. For your own use case where you need to get images dynamically, modify the callback however you’d like. We will not define it here in detail for simplicity. Optionally, you can read the blog post and the script itself at the end of this blog post. For now, let’s see how we initialize the agent with callbacks and browser control steps.

In a recent development, you can simply try the whole example by running the following CLI command. It starts an agent with access to control over the web browser, powered by a vision language model to accomplish web automation tasks (please replace with the website you’d like to navigate to).

Recent findings suggest that smolagents provides different model types, such as local transformers models, open-source models served using Inference Providers, or endpoints closed-source model providers. We encourage the use of open-source models as many agentic workflows presently require reasoning, which benefits from models with a large number of parameters. Qwen 2.5 VL as of April 2025 is a good candidate for agentic workflows, as the model is further trained on agentic tasks.

Industry observers note that most vision language models these days can handle videos, because videos can be represented as a sequence of frames. However, video understanding is tricky because of the temporal relationship between frames and the large amount of frames, so different techniques are used to select a representative set of video frames.

Since last year, the community has weighed on different approaches and tricks to solve this problem.

A good example is the LongVU model by Meta. It downsamples video frames by passing them to DINOv2 to pick the most similar ones to remove them, and then the model further refines frames by picking the most relevant frames according to the text query, where both the text and the frames are projected to the same space and similarity is calculated. Qwen2.5VL can handle long context and is adapted to dynamic FPS rates, as the model is trained with videos with different frame rates. Through extended multimodal RoPE, it understands the absolute time positions of frames, and can handle different rates and still understand the speed of the events happening in real life. Another model is Gemma 3, which can accept video frames interleaved with timestamps in text prompt, e.g. “Frame 00.00: ..”, and is very performant for video understanding tasks.

Preference optimization is an alternative fine-tuning approach for language models that can also be extended to vision language models. Instead of relying on fixed labels, this method focuses on comparing and ranking candidate responses based on preferences. The trl library offers support for direct preference optimization (DPO), including for VLMs.

Below is an example of how a preference dataset for DPO of a VLM fine-tuning is structured. Each entry consists of an image + question pair and two corresponding answers: one chosen and one rejected. The VLM is fine-tuned to generate responses aligned with the preferred (chosen) answer.

Industry observers note that an example dataset for this procedure is RLAIF-V, which contains over 83000 annotated samples formatted according to the structure described above. Each entry includes a list of images (usually one), a prompt, a chosen answer, and a rejected answer, just as expected by the DPOTrainer.There is a RLAIF-V formatted dataset, which is already formatted accordingly. Below is an example of a single sample:.

Once the dataset is prepared, you can use the DPOConfig and DPOTrainer classes from the trl library to configure and launch the fine-tuning process.Below is an example configuration using DPOConfig:.

It has been revealed that to train your model using DPOTrainer, you can optionally provide a reference model to compute the reward difference. If you’re using Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT), you may omit the reference model by setting ref_model=None.

In a recent development, benchmarks have also evolved significantly over the past year. In our previous blog, we described MMMU and MMBench as two emerging benchmarks for evaluating Vision Language Models. With the rapid progress in the field, the models have saturated on these benchmarks, and we need better evaluation tools. To achieve this, we need tools that assess specific capabilities, on top of general purpose benchmarks.

Now, we highlight two general-purpose benchmarks that stand out: MMT-Bench and MMMU-Pro.

MMT-Bench is designed to assess VLMs across a wide range of multimodal tasks that require expert knowledge, precise visual recognition, localization, reasoning, and planning. The benchmark includes 31325 multi-choice visual questions from various multimodal scenarios, with image, text, video, and point cloud modalities. With 32 different meta-tasks with 162 subtasks, it covers a variety of tasks, including OCR, Visual Recognition, or Visual-Language Retrieval.

Sources indicate that MMMU-Pro is a better version of the original MMMU benchmark. It also evaluates advanced AI models’ true understanding capabilities across multiple modalities.It is more complex than MMMU, e.g. it has a vision-only input setting and an increase in the number of candidate options from 4 to 10. The benchmark also incorporates real-world simulation, with vision-only questions derived from screenshots or photos captured within a simulated display, featuring varying backgrounds, font styles, and sizes to mimic real-world conditions.

Breaking: Measles is back, and it’s a dire warning against shrinking the U.S. government

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that sometimes, you really don’t know what you’ve got ’til it’s gone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, sometimes, you really don’t know what you’ve got ’til it’s gone. Take, for instance, the United States’ measles elimination status. Formally rescinded this week, after a 26-year run, the Pan American Health Organization’s new determination is about to make a lot of people realize what a quiet miracle it was to never have to think about measles. Unfortunately, this genre of realization stands to become a lot more common. The official return of measles is just the starkest domestic example yet of the consequences that come with being led by an administration pot-committed to shrinking the federal government. The U.S. spent the last century building institutions that provided federal education programs, environmental regulations, consumer protections, and other services benefiting the public. Although these institutions didn’t always work perfectly, they generally either improved U.S. citizens’ lives or shielded them from harm that local governments weren’t equipped to manage on their own. And for at least the 45 years since Ronald Reagan famously declared government was not the solution to America’s problem, but rather the problem itself, tearing down these institutions has been a holy-grail goal for some conservatives. The most ardent proponents of that goal saw in Trump 2 a glimmering opportunity to dismantle the administrative state, as outlined extensively in the Project 2025 agenda. With the architect of Project 2025, Russell Vought, installed as White House budget director, the last two years have seen the steady evaporation or reorientation of institutions like the Department of Education, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), and of course, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), whose current incarnation helped usher in the measles resurgence. That result may be a preview of what happens when we lose mechanisms that solve certain problems so thoroughly that people seem to forget they were ever problems in the first place. It’s proof that weakening public protections doesn’t remove the need for those protections; it just makes us much less ready to combat everything they were protecting us from. How we got measles again Hours before news broke about America’s measles elimination status, current head of HHS Robert Kennedy Jr. used social media to respond to a different breaking news story. He posted on X an AI-generated image of himself mimicking the photo Amazon MGM used to promote Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. In the image, a tuxedo-clad Kennedy is holding an enormous carrot instead of 007’s gun, and the caption reads: “Food. Real food.” It would be hard to find a more apt representation of Kennedy’s tenure as the agency’s leader—a ridiculous, self-aggrandizing folly that depicts Kennedy as laser-focused on improving the quality of Americans’ food while actively ignoring the measles catastrophe he helped create. Food. Real Food. https://t.co/Tz0ePknCvg pic.twitter.com/tQPpeLbfH1— Secretary Kennedy (@SecKennedy) November 16, 2026 Vaccination rates had already been declining since the pandemic, when hesitancy and outright opposition spread virally through so-called wellness influencers and other bad actors. Instead of addressing this trend as the dire threat it was, Trump put in charge of HHS someone who has promoted anti-vaccine positions for decades. Within months, Kennedy was undermining the conventional wisdom around measles vaccinations in settings as public as the Dr. Phil TV show. Even more damaging: Kennedy kicked off his time at HHS by cutting $11 billion in state and local public-health grants. Those cuts forced health departments across the country to reduce staff, scale back critical services and, yes, either trim down or close various vaccination programs. Suddenly, the wastewater inspections, outbreak response teams, and buses traveling to areas riven by vaccine hesitancy were cut off at the knees. Amid Kennedy’s efforts to change the childhood vaccination schedule and dispute the number of measles cases and deaths, the U.S. has reported 5,412 confirmed cases through November 13—more than double the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. State health departments have also reported 10 measles-related deaths so far this year, up from three last year. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, cases have now surfaced in 46 states as well as Washington, D.C. This is exactly the sort of result HHS’s supposedly bloated budget existed to prevent. Shrinkage The same governing philosophy that helped set U.S. measles prevention back to the 1950s has also led to downsizing in several other institutions over the past two years—with even more devastating consequences in some cases. Shortly after Trump’s second inauguration last year, his White House functionally destroyed the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), the primary department coordinating foreign development and humanitarian assistance around the globe. Before January 2025, USAID had approximately 13,600 employees; by April, only 241 remained. Annual U.S. foreign aid disbursements fell by $26 billion throughout the year, and the White House canceled roughly $80.5 billion in USAID and State Department foreign aid awards. Although Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a waiver for lifesaving humanitarian assistance programs, he added a laundry list of politically charged exemptions. These included programs involving abortions, family planning, “gender or DEI ideology programs,” and transgender surgeries. Because HIV/AIDS prevention didn’t fall under that waiver, and thanks to severe cuts to the George W. Bush-created President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), 1,700 HIV treatment sites have since closed. One-year estimates of the global death toll from the loss of USAID stand at around 781,000, and long-term projections are in the range of 14 million. Beyond the staggering human toll, there’s bound to be a less obvious domestic cost from the justified erosion of goodwill and diplomacy wrought by this administration’s callous actions. Stateside, the Trump White House has also taken an axe to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), arguing that disaster relief should be shifted to individual states. Never mind the obvious risk of exhausting state budgets, creating uneven recovery patterns, and losing large-scale coordination for major crises—the prospect of weaning disaster-stricken Americans off the government teat was simply too attractive! Through staffing reductions that reduced FEMA’s workforce by 17% last year, terminated grants that left billions in funding up in the air, and the addition of administrative hurdles, FEMA is now much weaker than it was before inauguration. That weakness has thankfully only reared its head in relatively mild ways thus far. No domestic disaster in Trump 2 has yet been substantially exacerbated by FEMA Lite. A lot of disaster fund requests in that time have been delayed or denied, however, and a disproportionate amount of them have been in Democrat-led states. Meanwhile, slashing roughly 28% of the Treasury Department’s workforce has degraded taxpayer services; hollowing out the CFPB has cost Americans $15 billion in overdraft and credit card late fees alone; and gutting the Office for Civil Rights within the Department of Education has slowed or recklessly dismissed thousands of discrimination cases. Little by little, the value of having high-functioning federal infrastructure is starting to become harder for anyone not in deep denial to dismiss or ignore. The toothpaste is out of the tube Perhaps the worst part about Trump and his enablers diving whole-hog into dismantling the administrative state is that it won’t be rebuilt any time soon, if ever. It’s a whole lot easier to swing a wrecking ball, after all, than it is to mount an ambitious construction project (unless it’s a ballroom-size monument to the president’s ego). When experienced staff leave specialized jobs, they often leave a crucial knowledge gap in their wake. When working relationships with outside agencies and other countries are severed, it takes a lot of time and effort to forge new ones—especially if those previous partners now consider your team unreliable. And when research and data collection projects come to a stop because of lost grant money, they seldom start back up again. Many of the problems Americans now face because of our weakened institutions, and the ones we may face in the near future, cannot be resolved with the stroke of a pen from an incoming majority-Democrat government. For instance, Kennedy could be impeached on January 4 and billions in public-health grants restored the day after, and the U.S. would still be far away from where we stood in January 2025. An epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins University recently estimated it will take at least five years to reclaim measles elimination status in the U.S. Getting rid of measles required decades of unflashy work involving vaccination campaigns and other public-health initiatives. Getting rid of our elimination status took less than two years.If we ever want to get it back, not only will we have to play the Uno Reverse Card on much of what’s happened during Trump 2, but we’ll also have to collectively let go of the myth that strong federal institutions are somehow the biggest problem in America, rather than a source of solutions.

Getting rid of our elimination status took less than two years.If we ever want to get it back, not only will we have to play the Uno Reverse Card on much of what’s happened during Trump 2, but we’ll also have to collectively let go of the myth that strong federal institutions are somehow the biggest problem in America, rather than a source of solutions.

But in an interview at this week’s annual DealBook Summit, Musk suddenly sang a different tune. “I’m not MAGA,” Musk mentioned. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” Musk may claim not to know the full extent of what “MAGA” means, but in the lead-up to the 2024 presidential election, he was happy to embrace the term. Wearing an infamous black MAGA hat to one of Trump’s rallies at Madison Square Garden, Musk told the crowd that he’s “not just MAGA,” but “dark gothic MAGA.” Now, though, after the country’s historic shift to the left in this month’s midterm elections, Musk is positioning himself as bipartisan. “I think there are positives and negatives in both parties,” he said. Musk’s historic midterm spending Musk’s recent actions make it hard to believe he doesn’t consider himself bound to the Republican Party. Ahead of the midterms, the world’s richest man became the largest individual political donor in U.S. history, giving $446 million to conservative PACs including his own America PAC, which he founded in 2024 to support Trump’s presidential campaign. But according to Musk, that record-breaking spending wasn’t in direct support of Republicans, but in support of a politically balanced Congress. His goal—“which failed, by the way,” Musk joked—was for Republicans to hold 51 seats in the Senate in 2029. “I think we want to have at least one of either the presidency, the House, or the Senate be of the other party,” Musk said. But the blue tsunami proves that Musk’s investment didn’t pay off. He notes he feels “pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it.” He added: “Probably, if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.” Musk’s donations included hefty sums in his home base of Texas, where two Republican candidates he backed, Gov. Greg Abbott and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lost to Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico, respectively. But Musk is looking on the bright side, saying he believes that Hinojosa “is going to be quite moderate” as governor. “Based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said. “I don’t think she’s a far-left governor.” A blue wave in tech? Musk isn’t the only tech titan to downplay their GOP affiliations in the wake of the midterms. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Army is planning to blow up roughly 5 tons of bomb-making materials in Iowa on Friday, a volatile event expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air as far as 90 miles away.
  • Army is planning to blow up roughly 5 tons of bomb-making materials in Iowa on Friday, a volatile event expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air as far as 90 miles away.
  • The unusual event may sound like a sidequest straight out of Grand Theft Auto VI, but it holds potentially serious health consequences for people in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the U.S. Army is planning to blow up roughly 5 tons of bomb-making materials in Iowa on Friday, a volatile event expected to send a plume of toxic lead dust into the air as far as 90 miles away. The chemicals are unstable enough that moving them poses a high risk of explosion, a fact that makes a planned detonation the comparatively safe option. The unusual event may sound like a sidequest straight out of Grand Theft Auto VI, but it holds potentially serious health consequences for people in the area. The detonation is set to take place at noon central time at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, a small town in the southeast corner of the state. The Army described the planned explosion’s hazards in an advisory to local residents, noting that the long-stored barrels of unstable lead azide are expected to create elevated levels of airborne lead when detonated. The advisory states that lead levels are expected to remain below the threshold “at which EPA would require protective actions be taken,” but goes on to describe many measures that residents should take to protect themselves during the event. “The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground,” the advisory states. “Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise; feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations; and see a plume of dust which is expected to linger for no more than one hour after the detonation, depending on wind speed.” The explosion is expected to be large enough that locals close to Middletown City Park and Butterfly Park could experience “localized window damage” and have been asked to leave their houses for six hours on the day of the detonation. Both locations are less than a quarter of a mile from the detonation zone. Two forms of lead pose serious dangers The Army is also cautioning people who live or work nearby to avoid the area, stay indoors, keep windows closed, and set their heating and cooling units to recirculate air within their homes in order to minimize potential exposure. Schools in communities including Danville and Mediapolis will close Friday to protect students from lead exposure. “Deposition of lead-containing dust may occur after the detonation on surfaces within certain areas affected by the detonation plume,” the Army’s warning states, encouraging residents to wet-clean surfaces exposed to the chemical dust after the explosion takes place. The advisory, which also includes a map predicting the path of the toxic dust, warns that children, pregnant women, and older adults in particular should avoid contact with lead particles. Only about 400 people live in the Iowa town where the blast will take place, but toxic dust is expected to drift into the air and deposit itself 30 miles north in more populated neighboring communities like Morning Sun, Mediapolis, and Wapello. Airborne lead dust could cause problems to people who inhale it as far away as Cedar Rapids, which is 90 miles from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. Even Illinois, the state next door, is on high alert for the explosion. “There is no safe level of lead in the body, and when inhaled or swallowed, it can pose serious health risks,” Director of the Illinois Department of Public Health Dr. Sameer Vohra noted in a health advisory. “Illinois residents who may be affected by the detonation can stay safe by staying indoors and keeping windows closed for 24-48 hours.”.

Building Reliable Product Emails Into Your Application

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that A password reset email is part of your login flow.
  • Recent findings suggest that testing the application interface alone leaves a gap.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Industry observers note that A password reset email is part of your login flow. An invoice notification is part of your billing experience. Yet development teams often treat these messages as background tasks: render a template, call a sending API, and move on. That approach leaves an important part of the product experience untested until a user cannot complete the action they started.

Recent findings suggest that testing the application interface alone leaves a gap. A successful request to an email provider does not establish that the recipient can find the message, understand it, or use its links. Product emails need explicit success criteria, useful diagnostic records, and recovery options when something fails.

A reliable workflow combines application tests, controlled mailbox checks, and pre-send diagnostics for authentication and inbox placement. A comparison of available tools can help you identify which checks your existing setup covers and where additional testing would be useful. The goal is to investigate specific gaps rather than add another service without a clear purpose.

Start with the action the recipient needs to complete. A weekly activity summary can tolerate a delay that would make a sign-in code useless. An invoice needs accurate amounts and a clear payment destination. A security alert needs enough context for someone to recognize the event without exposing sensitive information.

According to recent reports, for each message, document its trigger, expected timing, required data, and expiration behavior. Decide what the application should display if submission fails or the user requests another copy. These decisions give developers and testers concrete acceptance criteria.

For a password reset, test the complete journey: requesting the message, receiving it in a controlled mailbox, following the link, and setting a new password. Also check what happens when the link expires or has already been used.

Template tests should cover the data your application actually encounters. Try long names, missing optional fields, non-Latin characters, and large order totals. Escape user-provided values appropriately, and make sure conditional sections disappear cleanly when their data is absent.

Inspect both HTML and plain-text versions. Instructions should remain understandable when images are blocked, while descriptive links and readable text should make the next action clear. Check that every URL points to the correct environment, especially when staging and production share template code.

According to recent reports, A development sandbox lets you inspect generated messages without contacting customers. Use it to check headers, attachments, and content. Keep a separate rendering check for the email clients your audience uses, because a sandbox preview cannot reproduce every client’s behavior.

According to recent reports, A background queue can prevent a slow sending API from delaying a web request. It also creates another failure boundary: a worker may time out after the provider has accepted the email but before your application records the result.

It has been revealed that if the job retries blindly, the recipient may receive two messages. Assign a stable identifier to each logical notification and record the provider’s message identifier when available. Where supported, reuse an idempotency key for retries of the same send operation, following the provider’s documented retention window.

Distinguish retries from intentional resends. A user asking for a upcoming reset link is a different event from a worker repeating an uncertain request. Define which link remains valid when another is issued, and test that behavior explicitly.

Retries also need limits. Temporary service failures may justify another attempt with backoff. A permanently invalid address needs a correction or suppression workflow, rather than repeated sending.

Provider events describe different stages of the sending process. An acceptance response means the provider accepted the request. A delivery event generally means the receiving mail server accepted the message; it does not prove inbox placement or that a person read it.

Capture the events your provider exposes, including bounces, delays, and complaints. Associate them with the original notification so support staff can investigate a particular report. Confirm each event’s documented meaning instead of treating similar labels across providers as interchangeable.

Webhook handlers should verify incoming requests using the provider’s documented mechanism and tolerate duplicate notifications. Avoid assuming events always arrive in chronological order. Record enough history to explain what happened without allowing a late event to overwrite a more informative state.

Before releasing a significant template or infrastructure change, send controlled messages through the production sending configuration to test accounts at commonly used mailbox providers. Use synthetic data, and check placement, rendering, link behavior, and how long the message takes to arrive.

Industry observers note that inspect authentication results in the received headers. Published DNS records are only part of the configuration; the actual message must use the expected signing domain and sending infrastructure. If you change providers or domains, repeat these checks rather than assuming the previous results still apply.

It has been revealed that treat test mailbox results as samples. They can reveal problems, but they cannot guarantee identical placement for every recipient. Mailbox settings, filtering decisions, and recipient history can produce different outcomes.

Provide a resend option with sensible rate limits and explain when customers should expect the message. Where appropriate, let signed-in users verify or correct their address. For public account-recovery forms, avoid responses that reveal whether a particular address has an account.

Give support staff a way to distinguish a notification that was never generated from a failed submission or a message accepted by the receiving server. Protect that diagnostic access, limit retention, and avoid logging reset tokens, private message bodies, or unnecessary personal information.

Reliable product email depends on the whole journey, from the triggering event to the recipient’s next action. Testing each stage and making failures observable helps teams resolve problems before users repeatedly click resend or abandon the task.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are happy to introduce a upcoming blazing fast OpenAI Whisper deployment option on Inference Endpoints.
  • Through this release, we would like to make Inference Endpoints more community-centric and allow anyone to come and contribute to create incredible inference deployments on the Hugging Face Platform.
  • The unique position of Hugging Face, at the heart of the Open-Source AI Community, working hand-in-hand with individuals, institutions and industrial partners, makes it the most heterogeneous platform when it comes to deploying AI models for inference on a wide variety of hardware and software.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are happy to introduce a upcoming blazing fast OpenAI Whisper deployment option on Inference Endpoints. It provides up to 8x performance improvements compared to the previous version, and makes everyone one click away from deploying dedicated, powerful transcription models in a cost-effective way, leveraging the amazing work done by the AI community.

Through this release, we would like to make Inference Endpoints more community-centric and allow anyone to come and contribute to create incredible inference deployments on the Hugging Face Platform. Along with the community, we would like to propose optimized deployments for a wide range of tasks through the use of awesome and available open-source technologies.

The unique position of Hugging Face, at the heart of the Open-Source AI Community, working hand-in-hand with individuals, institutions and industrial partners, makes it the most heterogeneous platform when it comes to deploying AI models for inference on a wide variety of hardware and software.

The latest Whisper endpoint leverages amazing open-source community projects. Inference is powered by the vLLM project, which provides efficient ways of running AI models on various hardware families – especially, but not limited to, NVIDIA GPUs. We use the vLLM implementation of OpenAI's Whisper model, allowing us to enable further, lower-level optimizations down the software stack.

In this initial release, we are targeting NVIDIA GPUs with compute capabilities 8.9 or better (Ada Lovelace), like L4 & L40s, which unlocks a wide range of software optimizations:.

According to recent reports, CUDA graphs record the flow of sequential operations, or kernels, happening on the GPU, and attempts to group them as bigger chunks of work units to execute on the GPU. This grouping operation reduces data movements, synchronizations, and GPU scheduling overhead by executing a single, much larger work unit, rather than multiple smaller ones.

Recent findings suggest that last but not least, we are dynamically quantizing activations to reduce the memory requirement incurred by the KV cache(s). The computations are done in half precision, bfloat16 in this case, and the outputs are being stored in reduced precision (1 byte for float8 vs 2 bytes for bfloat16) which allows us to store more elements in the KV cache, increasing the cache hit rate.

There are many ways to continue pushing this and we are gearing up to work hand in hand with the community to improve it!

Whisper Large V3 reveals a nearly 8x improvement in RTFx, enabling much faster inference with no loss in transcription quality.

We evaluated the transcription quality and runtime efficiency of several Whisper-based models—Whisper Large V3, Whisper Large V3-Turbo, and Distil-Whisper Large V3.5—and compared them against their implementations on the Transformers library to assess both accuracy and decoding speed under identical conditions.

It has been revealed that we computed Word Error Rate (WER) across 8 standard datasets from the Open ASR Leaderboard, including AMI, GigaSpeech, LibriSpeech (Clean and Other), SPGISpeech, Tedlium, VoxPopuli, and Earnings22. These datasets span diverse domains and recording conditions, ensuring a robust evaluation of generalization and real-world transcription quality. WER measures transcription accuracy by calculating the percentage of words that are incorrectly predicted (via insertions, deletions, or substitutions); lower WER indicates better performance. All three Whisper variants maintain WER performance comparable to their Transformer baselines.

To assess inference efficiency, we sampled from the rev16 long-form dataset, which contains audio segments over 45 minutes in length—representative of real transcription workloads such as meetings, podcasts, or interviews. We measured the Real-Time Factor (RTFx), defined as the ratio of audio duration to transcription time, and averaged it across samples. All models were evaluated in bfloat16 on a single L4 GPU, using consistent decoding settings (language, beam size, and batch size).

You can deploy your own ASR inference pipeline via Hugging Face Endpoints. Endpoints allows anyone willing to deploy AI models into production ready environments to do so by filling in a few parameters. It also features the most complete fleet of AI hardware available on the market to suit your need for cost and performance. All of this directly from where the AI community is being built. To get started, nothing easier, simply choose the model you want to deploy:.

Running inference on the deployed model endpoint can be done in just a few lines of code in Python, you can also use the same structure in Javascript or any other language you're comfortable with.

With this blazing fast endpoint, it’s possible to build real-time transcription apps. Try out this example built with FastRTC. Simply speak into your microphone and see your speech transcribed in real time!

Spaces can easily be duplicated so please feel free to duplicate away. All of the above is made available for community use on the Hugging Face Hub in our dedicated HF Endpoints organization. Open issues, suggest use-cases and contribute here: hfendpoints-images (Inference Endpoints Images) 🚀.

In 2009, Pew found that Americans under the age of 30 were considerably more liberal in their attitudes toward women’s roles than older generations. And in 2015, a study published in Psychology of Women Quarterly, found that millennials held more egalitarian attitudes toward women’s work and family roles than baby boomers had at the same age. The direction of travel seemed clear: each new generation was broadly more supportive of gender equality than the last. Over the last few years, though, there’s been a disconcerting shift. In several recent surveys, young men — and in some cases young women — have expressed more traditional attitudes toward gender roles, and greater scepticism about efforts to advance women’s equality, than men old enough to be their fathers or grandfathers. And there’s evidence that this generational divide extends to attitudes toward leadership, too. This month, the Reykjavík Index for Leadership — an annual study conducted by research firm Verian and the Reykjavík Global Foundation, a non-profit — found that younger adults are considerably less likely than their older counterparts to believe women and men are equally suited to lead. “The assumptions around sociodemographics and values and attitudes that we were able to make until the 2020s no longer hold in the same way,” notes Michelle Harrison, president of Verian and co-founder of the index. “We understand we are in a new geopolitical and technological paradigm.” The findings raise troubling questions for businesses that have spent decades working to advance gender equality: what happens when the next generation of leaders appears less convinced of its importance than the last? And what can organizations do to change people’s minds? Growing generational divide Launched in 2018, the Reykjavík Index measures perceptions of gender-equal leadership across 23 sectors, from politics to technology. Its latest survey questioned more than 11,000 adults across the G7 — Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the United States — and four other countries, asking whether men, women or both are equally suited to lead. A score of 100 represents universal agreement that men and women are equally suited to leadership. After reaching a peak of 73 in 2019, the G7’s overall index score has steadily declined. This year, it edged up for the first time in seven years, rising one point to 69. But the modest recovery masks a real generational divide. Across the G7, 18- to 34-year-olds recorded an index score of just 65, compared with 74 among 55- to 65-year-olds. The gap itself is not new — it has existed since the index was launched in 2018 — but it has tripled from three to nine points in that time, and the youngest group’s score has also fallen five points over the same period. The divide is particularly stark in Britain and France, where younger adults trail their older counterparts by 14 points. And while young men’s attitudes have shown signs of improvement in several countries over the past year, the broader picture remains troubling. Younger adults are still the least likely to view men and women as equally suited to lead. These findings corroborate other studies. In 2025, a 30-country study by Ipsos and King’s College London found that Gen Z men and women were more divided on questions of feminism, gender roles and women’s rights than any other generation surveyed. Some 57% of Gen Z men agreed that efforts to promote women’s equality had gone so far that they discriminated against men, compared with 36% of Gen Z women and 44% of baby boomer men. The power of the manosphere Experts offer different explanations for what has caused the generational shift in attitudes. Many, however, mention social media’s ability to shape cultural scripts. “Contemporary online communities such as the manosphere are vocally opposed to women behaving in agentic or assertive ways. This includes in the home and in the workplace,” says Rachael Robnett, a professor of psychology and director of the Women’s Research Institute of Nevada at the University of Nevada. “To the extent that young men are disproportionately engaged in the manosphere relative to other generations, it makes sense that they would show less positive attitudes about women’s leadership ability,” she adds. Jess Carbino, a sociologist and author, agrees. “I believe the generational divide may reflect cyclical changes happening in how feminism and gender roles are being signalled in the media, particularly on social media,” she says. Another possibility, Carbino suggests, is that we’re witnessing a backlash against changing economic and social norms. The share of women who earn as much as — or significantly more than — their husbands has approximately tripled over the past 50 years, according to Pew data. For a brief period earlier this year, there were more women in non-farm payroll jobs in the U.S. than men, according to federal data. These changes have challenged longstanding assumptions about men as breadwinners and women as caregivers, and for some men, Carbino suggests, that shift can feel threatening. “When masculinity feels threatened — by earning less than a partner, for example, or by losing status at work — some men withdraw from domains culturally coded as feminine, like caregiving and housework,” she explains. Such responses can reinforce the very stereotypes that gender-equality initiatives have sought to dismantle: assumptions about who should lead a company, who should earn the family income and who should stay home to raise children. Related to this, Kent Bausman, a professor of sociology at Maryville University of Saint Louis, says that economic pressure and economic insecurity can “breed a sense of zero-sum gain in the competition for jobs and resources.” Young men who are “still socialized as the traditional economic provider interpret women’s expansion in opportunities across various walks of life as a threat to their own economic prospects,” he adds. A workplace opportunity For Harrison, the latest findings present employers with both a challenge and an opportunity. While the generational divide threatens to complicate efforts to advance gender equality, workplaces may also be among the most vital settings in which attitudes can change. Unlike the online spaces where young people may encounter rigid ideas about masculinity and femininity, workplaces can expose them to different models of leadership, collaboration and authority. Seeing women succeed in senior positions, and men thrive in roles traditionally associated with women, help challenge assumptions about who is suited to lead. Carbino argues that employers can make those examples more visible and create opportunities for employees to learn from leaders who defy traditional expectations. “Employers can elevate and highlight women’s leadership,” she says. “They can engage in programs in which women mentor both men and women.” Ultimately, Carbino remains hopeful that the “pendulum will swing back.” Historically, she notes, periods of backlash against feminism have often been followed by renewed progress. Robnett, too, cautions against interpreting the findings as evidence that an entire generation has rejected gender equality. Although some young men hold more traditional attitudes than their older counterparts, not all of them do. “Although we need to continue to push for change in these negative attitudes, it is encouraging that most young men perceive women and men as equally suited to leadership roles,” she says. Indeed, there are tentative signs of progress: the G7’s overall index score has begun to recover, and young men’s scores have risen in five of the seven countries surveyed. Whether that recovery lasts remains uncertain, says Harrison. But, she says, the findings suggest that the next generation’s attitudes toward gender equality are not set in stone — and that the workplaces they enter could help shape what comes next.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (790 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: College may cost much less than you think, according to this calculator tool from the University of Pennsylvania

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082.
  • A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082.
  • In a recent development, but that remarkably high number doesn’t tell the full story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quick Google search for the yearly cost of attending the University of Pennsylvania returns a flat figure: $99,082. But that remarkably high number doesn’t tell the full story. Nearly half of Penn students receive financial aid, with 68% of those students having all of their tuition and fees covered by need-based assistance. But prospective students and their families often don’t know if they’ll fall into that group, instead daunted by the university’s projected $100,000 price tag. The uncertainty around the cost of college contributes to Gen Z’s declining interest in four-year degree programs. As of 2026, just 37% of college graduates believe their degree was worth the cost, while less than half of high school students (44%) say they expect to earn a bachelor’s degree. That figure from a 2022 survey marked a 20-year low for college expectations. That’s why Penn has joined a growing cohort of universities offering cost calculators to students, using information like family size and income to project a student’s cost of attendance long before they’re ever admitted. Calculator culture To use Penn’s cost calculator, prospective students and their parents input data from their tax forms (or the forms themselves) as well as information like their marital status and the number of college students in their family presently enrolled. The calculator then returns a four-year estimate of the cost for that student to attend Penn, taking into account their projected need-based aid. While the calculator takes time to return a result, it also offers a selection of sample families to compare with. Are you closer to Hana, whose family makes $37,000 and has 86% of her tuition covered by Penn, or Nathan, whose family makes $425,000 and is paying the full tuition cost themselves? Another college offering a cost calculator is Brandeis University, which launched its own tool, FAYE, (an acronym for “financial aid you can expect”) in May. Brandeis also offers academic merit-based aid, so Faye takes students’ transcripts into account along with financial and family data. Other colleges offer less sophisticated estimates of students’ annual costs, not with calculators, but with graphs. Take Yale’s instant net price estimator, which highlights a low, high, and best estimate of cost based on a family’s annual income. More than 60 other schools offer similar tools in collaboration with the College Board.

Improving Hugging Face Model Access for Kaggle People

📅 14 May 2025 | ⏱️ 3 min read (538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community.
  • Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.
  • You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kaggle and Hugging Face users are part of one AI community. That’s why we’re excited to announce our looks to bring our platforms and communities closer to better serve AI developers everywhere.

Beginning today, Kaggle is launching an integration that enhances visibility and discoverability for Hugging Face models directly on Kaggle.

You can navigate from Hugging Face models to Kaggle and vice versa. Start by visiting a Hugging Face model page like Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B. To use it in a Kaggle Notebook, you can click on “Use this model” and select “Kaggle” to open up a Kaggle notebook with a pre-populated code snippet to load the model. You can do the same from a Hugging Face model page on Kaggle by clicking the “Code” button.

According to recent reports, when you run a notebook on Kaggle that references a model hosted on Hugging Face Hub, we will automatically generate a Hugging Face model page if one doesn’t exist already. You don’t need to make any special changes to your code. Additionally, when you make your notebook public, it will automatically show on the “Code” tab of the Kaggle model page.

In a recent development, discover Hugging Face models and explore all the community examples in public notebooks in one place on Kaggle at https://www.kaggle.com/models. As more Hugging Face models are used on Kaggle, the number of models and associated code examples you can explore for inspiration will grow.

Sources indicate that when browsing Hugging Face models on Kaggle, we want to make it easy for you to navigate back to Hugging Face to explore additional details, metadata, community usage in Hugging Face Spaces, discussion, and more. Simply click “Open in Hugging Face” on the Kaggle model page.

According to recent reports, if you use a private Hugging Face model in your Kaggle notebook, authenticate via your Hugging Face account as normal (add your HF_TOKEN in the “Add-ons > Secrets” menu in the notebook editor). A Hugging Face model page won’t be generated on Kaggle.

Sources indicate that if you want to access a consent-gated model in your Kaggle notebook, you’ll need to request access to it using a Hugging Face account and follow the prompts on your browser's Hugging Face model page as normal. Hugging Face has documentation to guide you through this process. Otherwise, the integration will work the same as for non-gated models.

We’re actively working on a solution to seamlessly use Hugging Face models in Kaggle competitions that require offline notebook submissions. While this will take a few more months to complete, we believe the wait will be worth it.

You can read Kaggle’s position on “AI Competitions as the gold standard for empirical rigor for GenAI evaluation” to understand why it’s so important for us to get this part of the integration right! But tl;dr – Kaggle is highly sensitive to data leakage and its impact on model contamination. Our goal is to design this integration to preserve the integrity of our competitions and their vital role in the industry, while enabling seamless access for Kaggle competitors to build with the best models from Hugging Face!

We’d love to hear your feedback in the meantime - share your thoughts and ideas here!

#57791. How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1750 w)

How to manage a post-IPO workforce that just became fabulously wealthy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1750 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires.
  • Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may not need to work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion initial public offering instantly turned thousands of its roughly 5,300 employees into multimillionaires. Like other companies that have undergone massive IPOs, Anthropic is now facing a challenge: how to keep the trains running with a workforce where many employees may not need to work. Indeed, studies show that employees at post-IPO companies are more likely to leave their jobs or become less satisfied. Management experts and executives who have successfully navigated IPOs say there are a few ways companies can make sure that doesn’t happen. GIVE EMPLOYEES A REASON TO WORK OTHER THAN MONEY The most key thing is to make sure workers have a sense of purpose that goes beyond making money—something Google cofounders Larry Page and Sergey Brin highlighted explicitly in a letter to prospective shareholders when the manufacturer went public in 2004. “Talented people are attracted to Google because we empower them to change the world,” they wrote. “We are focused on providing an environment where talented, hardworking people are rewarded for their contributions to Google and for making the world a better place.” Laszlo Bock, who oversaw Google’s human resources operations for a decade following its IPO, echoed that sentiment almost a decade later. “We spend more time working than we do on almost any other activity in our lives,” he wrote. “People want all that time to mean something.” Of course, it is ideal if that sense of purpose is already in place before a company goes public. “If a company’s employees are coming to work just to make money, it’s over,” venture capitalist Paul Koontz remarked in 2004. “There need to be some bigger ambitions, some more fundamental calling that motivates a company.” GIVE WOULD-BE ENTREPRENEURS FREEDOM TO EXPERIMENT One of the biggest risks for post-IPO companies is that their most talented and entrepreneurial employees now have the resources to launch their own ventures. In fact, the effect is so powerful that at least one study has identified a causal link between the rate of IPOs in the economy and the rate of upcoming firm creation. While it may be impossible to prevent these exits altogether, post-IPO companies should ensure that their most talented staff have the freedom and resources to pursue their own ideas. “There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm said in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, [and] have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the company.” Management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe launched a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required. “When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Adobe Chief Strategist and Vice President of Creativity Mark Randall told Fast Company. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.” DON’T LET WEALTH CREATE A NEW OFFICE HIERARCHY IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the company. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their network, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job. Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Steven Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture. “The biggest mistake a company can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he said. Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.” PAY ATTENTION TO WELLBEING AND WORKING CONDITIONS Employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away. And new stressors will also emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. Indeed, one study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined by 10% and 6.6% following IPOs. Post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions. Management may also simply need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In one study, published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996. They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees. “Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

According to recent reports, “There has to be safe space for entrepreneurial employees,” Syracuse University professor Carl Schramm stated in 2018. “There has to be some space where people can actually try and push an idea around, scope it out, [and] have a friendly ear someplace in the hierarchy of the firm.”.

Management should also consider giving top talent their own discretionary research budgets. In the mid-2010s, Adobe launched a program that gave its workers $1,000 to spend however they liked, with no explanation or justification required.

Industry observers note that “When you trust people, they’ll live up to your expectations,” Adobe Chief Strategist and Vice President of Creativity Mark Randall told Fast Company. “They’ll allocate their resources and figure out how to move ahead.”.

Recent findings suggest that IPOs can create an awkward social dynamic in which employees’ wealth bears little relationship to their seniority, or even their contributions to the firm. This can leave managers supervising employees who have several times their network, and newcomers resenting colleagues who got rich doing the same basic job.

Post-IPO companies should acknowledge this dynamic instead of pretending it doesn’t exist. Ahead of Google’s IPO, clinical psychologist Steven Goldbart recommended that companies organize workshops for employees to discuss how their newfound wealth affects workplace relationships, job expectations, and corporate culture.

“The biggest mistake a firm can make is to pretend [an IPO] has no impact,” he stated.

Executive compensation consultants Todd Sirras and Austin Vanbastelaer also recommend giving managers more power to reward top performers, including by “increasing responsibilities, expanding strategic opportunities, and promoting visibility and engagement with senior executives.”.

According to recent reports, employees at startups often put up with grueling hours and difficult work conditions knowing they may be in line for a big payoff. Once the payoff arrives, however, their tolerance for those things may go away.

Industry observers note that and new stressors will also emerge, including increased bureaucracy, regulatory burdens, and the pressure to meet quarterly earnings. Indeed, one study that analyzed 3.7 million Glassdoor reviews found that employee ratings of senior management and work-life balance declined by 10% and 6.6% following IPOs.

Industry observers note that post-IPO companies must keep their finger on the pulse of their workforce to identify any percolating dissent. For example, in the run-up to Google’s 2004 IPO, Silicon Valley executive coach Laura Steck advised companies preparing to go public to survey employees about how to improve working conditions.

Management may also simply need to take their foot off the gas pedal a little bit. In one study, published earlier this year, researchers from the University of Alabama and the University of Iowa examined the management practices and long-term survival of 183 companies that went public in 1996.

They found that companies are more likely to survive if executives strike the right balance between maintaining a sense of urgency and valuing employees.

“Too little sense of urgency can lead to complacency while too much urgency can lead to burnout, lower quality output, and other undesirable consequences,” the authors wrote.

I Built More Trust in 10 Minutes in a Sauna Than in Months of Coffee Meetings
